strengths: Identifies an important conceptual pitfall in the SAE literature: demonstrating that optimizing for reconstruction error at low L0 actively incentivizes the SAE to learn entangled/hedged feature representations that achieve lower MSE than the ground-truth dictionary.
The synthetic toy model experiment is clean, intuitive, and clearly demonstrates both the failure mode of low L0 (feature mixing / hedging) and high L0 (degenerate solutions).
Introduces a simple and computationally efficient diagnostic metric, the N-th decoder projection score ($s_n^{\text{dec}}$), which consistently identifies the true L0 in the synthetic setting.
Empirical findings on Gemma-2-2b show that the minimum of the $s_n^{\text{dec}}$ metric corresponds well with peak performance on the sparse probing benchmark (Kantamneni et al., 2025).
weaknesses: Empirical scope on language models is narrow: all LLM experiments are restricted to a single layer (layer 12) of a single model (Gemma-2-2b), a single width (32k), and a single architecture (BatchTopK). It is unclear how the optimal L0 scales across different layers, model sizes, or SAE expansion factors.

Theoretical and mechanistic justification for the metric $s_n^{\text{dec}}$ is somewhat informal. While the intuition for why projections are large when L0 is too low (feature hedging) is clear, the explanation for why $s_n^{\text{dec}}$ increases when L0 is too high (degenerate mixtures) is not fully formalized or thoroughly analyzed.

Evaluation relies almost entirely on sparse probing for Gemma-2-2b. Evaluating feature interpretability via auto-interpretability scoring, feature absorption metrics, or downstream steering/ablation would significantly strengthen the claim that features at L0=200-250 are more monosemantic than those at lower L0.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely question in mechanistic interpretability regarding whether target sparsity (L0) in sparse autoencoders (SAEs) should be treated merely as a Pareto trade-off parameter or if there is an optimal operating point for feature disentanglement.

The synthetic toy experiment clearly demonstrates the failure mode: when the enforced L0 is lower than the true active feature count, MSE reconstruction actively incentivizes the SAE to learn polysemantic mixtures of correlated features to reduce residual variance.
The paper introduces an intuitive decoder projection metric ($s_n^{dec}$) to detect feature over-mixing and evaluates it against downstream sparse probing benchmarks on Gemma-2-2b.
weaknesses: The submission is severely underdeveloped for a full conference paper: the main body spans only 4 pages before the references, leaving key discussions, methodological formalisms, and evaluations truncated or relegated to the appendix.

Empirical evaluation on language models is extremely narrow, restricted to only a single layer (layer 12) of a single model (Gemma-2-2b) and a single SAE architecture (BatchTopK). Without evaluation across multiple architectures (e.g., standard TopK, JumpReLU, L1-regularized SAEs), layers, and model families, the claim that LLM SAEs universally exhibit a clear 'true L0' around 200–250 is not convincingly established.

The proposed decoder projection score ($s_n^{dec}$) lacks rigorous theoretical justification and relies heavily on heuristics. Its sensitivity to the choice of the rank hyperparameter $N$ (inconsistently labeled as $k$ in Figure 3 and Figure 10, colliding with TopK notation) is substantial, and the curve for high $N$ appears mostly flat after reaching the minimum rather than having a distinct optimum.

The correlation between the minimum of $s_n^{dec}$ and the peak in sparse probing F1 score (Figure 4) may simply reflect the known property that higher L0 retains more signal capacity until overparameterization/noise sets in; the drop in sparse probing performance at higher L0 is very marginal (less than 0.02 F1 score) and lacks error bars or statistical significance tests.

Presentation and completeness issues: on page 2, the manuscript contains an incomplete placeholder ('Our code is available at '), and notations between the text ($n, N$) and figure titles ($k$) are inconsistent.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and fundamental question in mechanistic interpretability: whether sparsity (L0) in Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) is merely an arbitrary Pareto-tradeoff hyperparameter or if there is a 'correct' operating regime.

The synthetic toy model (Section 3 and Appendix A.2) cleanly illustrates the failure mode of low L0: when L0 is constrained below the true number of active features, MSE loss actively incentivizes the SAE to learn entangled, correlated feature mixtures ('hedging') that achieve lower reconstruction error than the ground-truth dictionary.
The proposed decoder projection metric ($s_n^{	ext{dec}}$) shows a clear minimum at the true L0 in the synthetic setting and correlates with peak sparse probing performance on Gemma-2-2b layer 12.
weaknesses: The empirical validation on language models is extremely narrow, evaluating only a single layer (layer 12) of a single model (Gemma-2-2b) with a single width (32k) and architecture (BatchTopK). Because the central claim argues that current open-source SAEs widely use suboptimal L0 values, evaluating across different model families (e.g., Llama, GPT-2), layers, and dictionary expansion factors is essential to substantiate generality.

The conceptual assumption of a single discrete 'true L0' in real LLMs is contentious and underdeveloped. Unlike synthetic setups with orthogonal base features, LLM activations exhibit multi-scale representations, hierarchical features, and feature splitting. Attributing the peak in probing performance to a single ground-truth L0 requires deeper theoretical justification.

The decoder projection score ($s_n^{	ext{dec}}$) lacks theoretical derivation. Furthermore, Figure 10 reveals that the metric's behavior is sensitive to the choice of $N$: for smaller $k$ ($k \le 500$), the curve exhibits entirely different dynamics compared to large $k$ ($k \ge 5000$), leaving the criterion for selecting $N$ largely heuristic.

The downstream evaluation relies solely on sparse probing F1 score. Probing improvements at higher L0 can be confounded by increased capacity / preservation of residual information rather than feature purity. Additional evaluations—such as automated interpretability scoring, monosemanticity metrics, or causal intervention/steering—are needed to verify that the latents learned at L0 = 200–250 are genuinely cleaner and less polysemantic.

The submission is under 5 pages of main text and omits important presentation elements (e.g., Section 2 leaves 'Our code is available at' blank, and the online optimization method in Appendix A.4 remains unstable and preliminary).

strengths: Identifies a critical flaw in current SAE evaluation practices: the paper convincingly demonstrates that evaluating SAEs along a sparsity–reconstruction (L0 vs. MSE/variance explained) Pareto curve is fundamentally misleading, as lower-than-true L0 actively incentivizes models via MSE loss to mix correlated features (feature hedging) and outperform ground-truth features on reconstruction.

The synthetic toy model experiments are clean, transparent, and provide direct ground-truth evidence showing how both positively and negatively correlated features are mixed into polysemantic latents when L0 is underestimated.

Proposes simple, unsupervised diagnostic proxy metrics (the $n$-th decoder projection score $s_n^{\text{dec}}$ and decoder pairwise cosine similarity) that do not require ground-truth labels and can be computed directly from activations and the decoder.
Empirical validation on Gemma-2-2B and Llama-3.2-1B shows that the 'elbow' / minimum of the proposed metric aligns well with peak downstream $k$-sparse probing performance across over 100 tasks.

Provides a practical and impactful take-home message for the mechanistic interpretability community, suggesting that many widely used open-source SAEs (which often target $L_0 < 100$) may be operating in a severely feature-hedging regime.
weaknesses: The proposed proxy metric $s_n^{\text{dec}}$ relies on heuristic choices, specifically the rank index $n$ (heuristically set near $h/2$), and the resulting curve does not always present a distinct global minimum in real models (often manifesting as a flat plateau or an 'elbow' that requires visual inspection).

The paper does not provide an end-to-end training method that reliably finds the optimal $L_0$ online; as noted in Appendix A.6, gradient-based meta-optimization of $L_0$ during training is unstable and requires heavy hyperparameter tuning, meaning practitioners must still train expensive sweeps across multiple $L_0$ values.

Evaluation on LLMs is restricted to two relatively small open models (Gemma-2-2B and Llama-3.2-1B) at a small selection of layers (5, 7, 12). While sparse probing is evaluated, direct qualitative or automated interpretability scoring (e.g., auto-interp fuzzing / monosemanticity scores) on the learned latents at different $L_0$ values in LLMs would have further reinforced the claim of feature degradation.

strengths: Important conceptual critique of current evaluation standards: The paper clearly demonstrates that evaluating SAEs purely along a sparsity–reconstruction Pareto frontier is flawed. Specifically, when L0 is constrained below the true number of active features, MSE actively favors feature hedging/mixing over the true disentangled features.

Clean and convincing toy model demonstrations: The synthetic experiments (Figures 1–5) provide compelling evidence that ground-truth dictionary features yield significantly worse reconstruction error than mixed, polysemantic features under low-L0 constraints, making the underlying failure mechanism intuitive and transparent.

Strong practical relevance to the interpretability community: The analysis suggests that many widely utilized public SAE checkpoints (e.g., on Neuronpedia / Gemma Scope) operate at an L0 that is too low, providing an explanatory hypothesis for why low-L0 SAEs often underperform on downstream probing and steering benchmarks.

Validation on open LLMs: The paper validates the connection between the proposed diagnostic metric (and decoder pairwise cosine similarity) and downstream k-sparse probing performance on Gemma-2-2B and Llama-3.2-1B.
weaknesses: Heuristic nature and sensitivity of the proposed metric: The n-th decoder projection metric ($s_n^{\text{dec}}$) relies heavily on the choice of $n$ (suggested empirically around $h/2$). Furthermore, as shown in Appendix A.9, the metric does not consistently yield a well-defined global minimum in LLMs, often requiring qualitative identification of an 'elbow' region.

Difficulty in automatic optimization: While Appendix A.6 proposes an online optimization method to select L0 dynamically during training, the authors acknowledge it requires delicate hyperparameter tuning and is unstable in real LLMs, leaving the search for L0 dependent on expensive sweeps.

Conceptual ambiguity of 'True L0' in natural language representations: In synthetic data with independent or correlated Bernoulli latents, a ground-truth L0 is well-defined. In real LLMs, however, concepts exist along a continuous hierarchy and varying levels of abstraction. The peak in k-sparse probing could partly reflect probe capacity rather than identifying an exact underlying discrete feature count; this distinction warrants deeper discussion.

Limited architectural and layer coverage: Evaluations on real models are restricted to isolated layers of small models (Gemma-2-2B layers 5 & 12, Llama-3.2-1B layer 7). Evaluating across different activation sites (residual stream vs. MLP post-activations) and larger models would substantiate the generality of the observed L0 threshold ranges.
Missing code link: The code repository link in the introduction is left blank ('Code is available at').

strengths: Compelling critique of the standard sparsity–reconstruction tradeoff: The paper convincingly demonstrates that when L0 is forced below the true number of active features, an SAE with the ground-truth dictionary incurs higher MSE than a model that mixes correlated features. This provides a clear explanation for why standard Pareto frontier plots can favor degenerate or polysemantic dictionaries.

Clean synthetic validation: The toy model experiments in Section 3 isolate the mechanics of feature hedging effectively, clearly distinguishing the effects of positive versus negative feature correlations on decoder representations.

Empirical connection to downstream interpretability benchmarks: The paper bridges toy findings to real LLMs (Gemma-2-2B and Llama-3.2-1B) by showing that the heuristic elbow/minimum in decoder projections corresponds well with peak k-sparse probing performance, offering practical relevance.

Actionable implication for the community: The observation that many widely used open-source SAEs (e.g., on Neuronpedia) operate at an L0 below 100, which may place them in the harmful feature-mixing regime, is important for practitioners in mechanistic interpretability.
weaknesses: Heuristic nature and sensitivity of the proposed metric: The n-th decoder projection metric s_n^dec relies on choosing an index n (empirically set around h/2). As shown in Appendix A.9, the shape of the metric curve varies substantially across different n values and layers, often showing a flat or shallow plateau rather than a crisp global minimum, making automated or unambiguous identification of the optimal L0 difficult.

Lack of a practical online tuning solution: While Appendix A.6 attempts an automatic adaptive L0 adjustment algorithm during training, the authors note it requires heavy hyperparameter tuning and is unstable in real LLMs. Consequently, finding the optimal L0 still necessitates expensive training sweeps across multiple L0 values.

Limited evaluation scope across layers and models: LLM evaluations are restricted to only a couple of specific layers (Gemma-2-2B layer 5/12 and Llama-3.2-1B layer 7). Given layer-to-layer variation in representation geometry and feature density, broader verification across diverse layers and larger model scales would strengthen the generality of the claims.

Minor presentation omissions and typos: The repository link under Section 1 is blank ('Code is available at '), and there are several typos throughout the text (e.g., 'monsemantic' in Figure 1, 'aleviating', 'increses' on page 21).
